content.content:
1	# Users
2	
3	A self-growing wiki of the people who use (or would use) this extension, and how
4	— usage patterns, personas, and pain points. Its sibling wikis cover the other
5	tools chasing the same job ([`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md))
6	and the broader calendar-market context these users sit in
7	([`../Market/`](../Market/README.md)).
8	
9	## Key insights
10	
11	- Every extractor request so far was filed by the repo owner — no outside user has ever reported a miss.
12	- The in-product report channel opens a prefilled GitHub issue, so reporting at all needs a GitHub account.
13	- What blocks a fix is usually page capture, not extraction: sites that 403 datacenter IPs can't be recorded.
14	- Reported demand skews to Israeli and civic sites, not the global ticketing platforms.
15	- Industry data backs the privacy persona: most top Chrome extensions ask for high-risk permissions at install.
16	- Because the extension refuses to guess a timezone, expect "no timezone" complaints, not "wrong time" ones.
17	- The personas here are still hypotheses — no review, support request or outside feedback has landed yet.
18	
19	## How this wiki grows
20	
21	Same mechanic as Market — the Claudinite **product-wiki** pack's growth worker
22	(mounted read-only under `.claudinite/`), following the "LLM Wiki" pattern:
23	compile once, refine in place, cite sources,
24	never silently overwrite.
25	
26	## Personas (initial pass — refine as real usage signal appears)
27	
28	- **The one-click saver.** Reads about a single event (a concert, a talk, a
29	  meetup) somewhere on the web and wants it on their calendar before they forget,
30	  with the least possible friction — no typing, no new account, no app switch.
31	  This is the extension's primary target today (see `product-requirements/`
32	  requirement 1).
33	- **The event browser.** Lands on a listing/series page with several events and
34	  wants to cherry-pick a few — served by the "one button per event" requirement.
35	- **The privacy-conscious user.** Actively avoids extensions that want an OAuth
36	  grant, an account, or send page content to a third-party AI API just to copy a
37	  date into a calendar. This persona is who the "no sign-in, no API key" product
38	  requirement is *for* — see the positioning notes in
39	  [`../Competitors/README.md`](../Competitors/README.md). This concern is
40	  well-grounded, not niche: 2026 studies report **86% of the top-100 Chrome
41	  extensions request high-risk permissions at install**, **52% of AI-branded
42	  extensions collect user data** (~1 in 3 collecting PII), and **71% of extensions
43	  publish no privacy policy** — and Chrome grants permissions at install that
44	  persist across every future update. A rule-based, no-OAuth, no-API-key,
45	  nothing-leaves-the-browser design answers exactly this anxiety.
46	
47	## Usage patterns
48	
49	- Single click → review pre-filled Google Calendar event → save. The extension
50	  deliberately stops short of auto-saving, so the user always reviews before
51	  committing (see `dev/requirements/requirements.md`).
52	- Works from whatever page the user is already on — no search, no lookup, no
53	  separate "paste a URL" step, unlike several competitor tools (see
54	  `../Competitors/README.md`).
55	
56	## Reported-demand signal (repo-native, last refreshed 2026-09-20)
57	
58	The first *observable* answer to "which misses actually get reported" — and it is
59	mostly a negative one. As of 2026-09-20 the repo carries **15 issues labelled
60	[`extractor-request`](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues?q=label%3Aextractor-request)**
61	(up from 14 on 2026-08-23), and **every one was filed by the repo owner**
62	(`missingbulb`) — the same owner-only pattern that held at 13 on 2026-08-09,
63	14 on 2026-08-23, and now 15 one month later. No external reporter appears
64	anywhere in that set. So the personas and pain points below still rest on
65	zero outside feedback; what follows is signal about the *channel* and about
66	one person's browsing, not about a user base.
67	
68	- **The channel exists, is in-product, and fires at the failure moment — but it
69	  is gated behind a GitHub account.** The popup's unsupported-host states carry
70	  two affordances (`extension/events-popup/source-request-view.js`): a "Suggest
71	  Correction" link when the generic extractor found a complete event on an
72	  unlisted host, and a "Disagree?" link that expands an inline "how this
73	  extension finds events" explanation ending in "open an issue". Both land the
74	  user on the repo's prefilled `extractor-request` issue form in a new tab —
75	  "no token, form service, or backend involved". Note the design *changed* from
76	  what was originally asked for: issue
77	  [#96](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/96)
78	  specified an **embedded Google Form** in the empty state, and the shipped
79	  implementation is a GitHub issue form instead, because GitHub forbids framing
80	  its pages (`X-Frame-Options`). The consequence for this wiki is the point: a
81	  reporter must be a logged-in GitHub user. That is a plausible — and
82	  **unverified** — explanation for why the external-report count is zero, and it
83	  is a friction this product otherwise spends all its design budget removing.
84	- **Reported demand skews local and civic, not global-platform.** Of the
85	  thirteen site-specific requests (twelve plus the newest,
86	  [#1118](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/1118),
87	  filed 2026-08-31), **nine now name Israeli hosts** (`tel-aviv.gov.il`,
88	  `comy.co.il`, `cinema.co.il`, `secrettelaviv.com`, `barby.co.il`,
89	  `eventim.co.il`, `thinkdrink.co.il`, `ticketmaster.co.il` — the local edition
90	  of a global platform — and now `tzavta.co.il`, a Tel Aviv performance venue),
91	  against only two genuinely international ones (`axs.com`, `bandsintown.com`).
92	  With a single reporter this is one person's browsing rather than a market
93	  shape, but it is worth holding as a hypothesis: the pages a person actually
94	  wants on their calendar are the small civic and venue sites near them, which
95	  are also the sites least likely to be served by a general AI tool trained on
96	  the majors.
97	- **A reported miss can be unfixable for reasons the user never sees — and the
98	  blocker is page *capture*, not extraction.** The `axs.com` request
99	  ([#285](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/285))
100	  was abandoned: AXS returns HTTP 403 to CI runners and the sandbox, so no real
101	  page HTML could be recorded, the pipeline refuses to invent `expected` values
102	  for a test case, and the owner closed it with *"Can't get the html to write an
103	  extractor for."* The `bandsintown.com` request
104	  ([#170](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/170))
105	  hit the identical 403 wall — the extractor was written but left uncompleted
106	  until a real browser supplied the page, after which it landed
107	  ([PR #199](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/pull/199)).
108	  So the sites most aggressive about bot-blocking are the ones least likely to
109	  gain a dedicated extractor, and from the user's side this looks like an
110	  arbitrary, permanent "no events found".
111	- **The channel also gets used for a second, quieter purpose: hardening
112	  coverage on an already-supported site, not just reporting a miss.** The one
113	  new `extractor-request` since 2026-08-09 —
114	  [#880](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/880),
115	  `edfringe.com`, filed 2026-08-11 — reads like the other twelve site-specific
116	  requests, but `edinburghfringe.js` had already existed since the 2026-06-22
117	  extractor restructure; the PR that closed it,
118	  [#881](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/pull/881),
119	  added a second recorded page, hardening an extractor that was already
120	  shipping, not new site support. Excluded from the local/civic-skew count
121	  below for that reason (it isn't a new-host demand signal), but it is a real
122	  use of the same form, filed by the same owner — the channel's only
123	  documented user treats it as a general-purpose "make this extractor better"
124	  form as much as a "this site doesn't work" one.
125	
126	## Pain points to track (hypotheses — verify with real feedback as it arrives)
127	
128	- Extraction misses or gets a field wrong on a page with unusual markup — the
129	  weekly
130	  [`generic-extractor-improvements`](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/blob/main/.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/generic-extractor-improvements/task.md)
131	  task (named `fallback-extractor-improvements` until the 2026-07-26 restructure
132	  retired the "fallback" vocabulary) is the engineering mechanism that narrows
133	  this over time; this wiki tracks it from the *user* side (which misses actually
134	  get reported/matter).
135	- Timezone correctness on pages that don't declare one clearly — see the
136	  unanimity rule in the contract header of
137	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js` (a zone is emitted only
138	  when two independent page-declared hints agree, otherwise none). The
139	  `technicalGotchas.md` this line cited until 2026-07-26 was superseded when that
140	  doc was folded into the gcec pack; the rule did **not** move into that pack's
141	  RULES.md, it lives in the source file's own header. A wrong `ctz` is a
142	  trust-breaking failure mode worth watching from the user's perspective — and
143	  because the contract refuses to guess, the *user-visible* failure is usually a
144	  **missing** timezone rather than a wrong one, so the complaint shape to expect
145	  in feedback is "it didn't set the timezone", not "it set the wrong time".
146	- No support yet for calendars other than Google Calendar (see Market's open
147	  question on Outlook/ICS) — track whether this actually blocks real users or is
148	  a hypothetical gap.
149	- **A site that blocks automated fetching stays unsupported indefinitely**, and
150	  the user is never told why. Verified 2026-08-09 on `axs.com` and
151	  `bandsintown.com` (see the reported-demand section above): the request path
152	  needs a captured copy of the page to write a test case against, and a site
153	  that returns HTTP 403 to datacenter IPs never yields one. This is a distinct
154	  pain point from "unusual markup" above — the extraction is not the hard part.
155	- **Reporting a miss requires a GitHub account.** The in-product "Suggest
156	  Correction" / "open an issue" affordances open the repo's prefilled issue form
157	  (`extension/events-popup/source-request-view.js`), so a user without a GitHub
158	  login has no way to report at all. Watch whether this is what keeps outside
159	  reports at zero.
160	
161	## Open questions
162	
163	- Do real users cite privacy/permissions as a *reason for choosing* a lightweight
164	  extension, or is it a latent preference they don't act on? (The permission-risk
165	  data above is industry-wide, not this extension's own user feedback.)
166	- ~~Which extraction misses actually get reported vs. silently tolerated — i.e.
167	  which sites matter enough to users to warrant a dedicated extractor?~~
168	  **Answered in the negative, 2026-08-09**: all 13 `extractor-request` issues to
169	  date are the repo owner's, so *no* miss has ever been reported by an outside
170	  user. The question that replaces it is the one below, about the channel.
171	- **Is the GitHub-account gate what keeps outside reports at zero?** The only
172	  report path is a prefilled GitHub issue form (see the reported-demand section).
173	  Worth deciding whether a no-account channel is worth building, or whether the
174	  zero simply reflects a small install base — the two are indistinguishable from
175	  inside the repo, and install counts are still unobtainable (see
176	  [`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md)'s standing open question).
177	  Surfaced 2026-08-09.
178	- **Is the local/civic skew in reported demand a property of the demand or of
179	  the single reporter?** Nine of thirteen site requests now name Israeli hosts
180	  (up from eight of twelve — see the 2026-09-20 refresh below). If it is real,
181	  it argues the product's edge is small venue and civic sites rather than the
182	  ticketing majors an AI competitor covers by default; if it is just one
183	  person's browsing, it should not steer extractor priorities. Only outside
184	  reports can separate the two. Surfaced 2026-08-09.
185	- Does the lack of non-Google-Calendar support actually block real users? (Pairs
186	  with Market's `.ics`-export note.)
187	- On timezone, which complaint shape actually shows up — "wrong time" or "no
188	  timezone at all"? The refusal-to-guess contract predicts the latter dominates;
189	  no real feedback yet either way (surfaced 2026-07-26).
190	
191	## Sources
192	
193	Personas and pain points above are hypotheses seeded from the product's existing
194	design decisions (`dev/procedures/highLevelDesign.md`,
195	`dev/requirements/requirements.md`) and general competitor positioning (see
196	`../Competitors/README.md`'s sources) — not yet from direct user research. Flag this
197	clearly until real user feedback (reviews, issues, support requests) backs a
198	claim here. The one externally-sourced claim so far is the industry
199	permission/privacy data backing the privacy-conscious persona:
200	
201	- [Ranking AI-Powered Chrome Extensions by Privacy Risk in 2026 (Incogni)](https://blog.incogni.com/chrome-extensions-privacy-2026/)
202	- [Chrome Permissions Statistics 2026 (AboutChromebooks)](https://www.aboutchromebooks.com/chrome-permissions-statistics/)
203	- [Enterprise Browser Extension Security Report 2026 (LayerX)](https://go.layerxsecurity.com/browser-extension-security-report-2026)
204	
205	The 2026-08-09 pass added the first *repo-native* user-side evidence — the

# Users

A self-growing wiki of the people who use (or would use) this extension, and how
— usage patterns, personas, and pain points. Its sibling wikis cover the other
tools chasing the same job ([`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md))
and the broader calendar-market context these users sit in
([`../Market/`](../Market/README.md)).

## Key insights

- Every extractor request so far was filed by the repo owner — no outside user has ever reported a miss.
- The in-product report channel opens a prefilled GitHub issue, so reporting at all needs a GitHub account.
- What blocks a fix is usually page capture, not extraction: sites that 403 datacenter IPs can't be recorded.
- Reported demand skews to Israeli and civic sites, not the global ticketing platforms.
- Industry data backs the privacy persona: most top Chrome extensions ask for high-risk permissions at install.
- Because the extension refuses to guess a timezone, expect "no timezone" complaints, not "wrong time" ones.
- The personas here are still hypotheses — no review, support request or outside feedback has landed yet.

## How this wiki grows

Same mechanic as Market — the Claudinite **product-wiki** pack's growth worker
(mounted read-only under `.claudinite/`), following the "LLM Wiki" pattern:
compile once, refine in place, cite sources,
never silently overwrite.

## Personas (initial pass — refine as real usage signal appears)

- **The one-click saver.** Reads about a single event (a concert, a talk, a
  meetup) somewhere on the web and wants it on their calendar before they forget,
  with the least possible friction — no typing, no new account, no app switch.
  This is the extension's primary target today (see `product-requirements/`
  requirement 1).
- **The event browser.** Lands on a listing/series page with several events and
  wants to cherry-pick a few — served by the "one button per event" requirement.
- **The privacy-conscious user.** Actively avoids extensions that want an OAuth
  grant, an account, or send page content to a third-party AI API just to copy a
  date into a calendar. This persona is who the "no sign-in, no API key" product
  requirement is *for* — see the positioning notes in
  [`../Competitors/README.md`](../Competitors/README.md). This concern is
  well-grounded, not niche: 2026 studies report **86% of the top-100 Chrome
  extensions request high-risk permissions at install**, **52% of AI-branded
  extensions collect user data** (~1 in 3 collecting PII), and **71% of extensions
  publish no privacy policy** — and Chrome grants permissions at install that
  persist across every future update. A rule-based, no-OAuth, no-API-key,
  nothing-leaves-the-browser design answers exactly this anxiety.

## Usage patterns

- Single click → review pre-filled Google Calendar event → save. The extension
  deliberately stops short of auto-saving, so the user always reviews before
  committing (see `dev/requirements/requirements.md`).
- Works from whatever page the user is already on — no search, no lookup, no
  separate "paste a URL" step, unlike several competitor tools (see
  `../Competitors/README.md`).

## Reported-demand signal (repo-native, last refreshed 2026-09-20)

The first *observable* answer to "which misses actually get reported" — and it is
mostly a negative one. As of 2026-09-20 the repo carries **15 issues labelled
[`extractor-request`](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues?q=label%3Aextractor-request)**
(up from 14 on 2026-08-23), and **every one was filed by the repo owner**
(`missingbulb`) — the same owner-only pattern that held at 13 on 2026-08-09,
14 on 2026-08-23, and now 15 one month later. No external reporter appears
anywhere in that set. So the personas and pain points below still rest on
zero outside feedback; what follows is signal about the *channel* and about
one person's browsing, not about a user base.

- **The channel exists, is in-product, and fires at the failure moment — but it
  is gated behind a GitHub account.** The popup's unsupported-host states carry
  two affordances (`extension/events-popup/source-request-view.js`): a "Suggest
  Correction" link when the generic extractor found a complete event on an
  unlisted host, and a "Disagree?" link that expands an inline "how this
  extension finds events" explanation ending in "open an issue". Both land the
  user on the repo's prefilled `extractor-request` issue form in a new tab —
  "no token, form service, or backend involved". Note the design *changed* from
  what was originally asked for: issue
  [#96](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/96)
  specified an **embedded Google Form** in the empty state, and the shipped
  implementation is a GitHub issue form instead, because GitHub forbids framing
  its pages (`X-Frame-Options`). The consequence for this wiki is the point: a
  reporter must be a logged-in GitHub user. That is a plausible — and
  **unverified** — explanation for why the external-report count is zero, and it
  is a friction this product otherwise spends all its design budget removing.
- **Reported demand skews local and civic, not global-platform.** Of the
  thirteen site-specific requests (twelve plus the newest,
  [#1118](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/1118),
  filed 2026-08-31), **nine now name Israeli hosts** (`tel-aviv.gov.il`,
  `comy.co.il`, `cinema.co.il`, `secrettelaviv.com`, `barby.co.il`,
  `eventim.co.il`, `thinkdrink.co.il`, `ticketmaster.co.il` — the local edition
  of a global platform — and now `tzavta.co.il`, a Tel Aviv performance venue),
  against only two genuinely international ones (`axs.com`, `bandsintown.com`).
  With a single reporter this is one person's browsing rather than a market
  shape, but it is worth holding as a hypothesis: the pages a person actually
  wants on their calendar are the small civic and venue sites near them, which
  are also the sites least likely to be served by a general AI tool trained on
  the majors.
- **A reported miss can be unfixable for reasons the user never sees — and the
  blocker is page *capture*, not extraction.** The `axs.com` request
  ([#285](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/285))
  was abandoned: AXS returns HTTP 403 to CI runners and the sandbox, so no real
  page HTML could be recorded, the pipeline refuses to invent `expected` values
  for a test case, and the owner closed it with *"Can't get the html to write an
  extractor for."* The `bandsintown.com` request
  ([#170](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/170))
  hit the identical 403 wall — the extractor was written but left uncompleted
  until a real browser supplied the page, after which it landed
  ([PR #199](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/pull/199)).
  So the sites most aggressive about bot-blocking are the ones least likely to
  gain a dedicated extractor, and from the user's side this looks like an
  arbitrary, permanent "no events found".
- **The channel also gets used for a second, quieter purpose: hardening
  coverage on an already-supported site, not just reporting a miss.** The one
  new `extractor-request` since 2026-08-09 —
  [#880](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/880),
  `edfringe.com`, filed 2026-08-11 — reads like the other twelve site-specific
  requests, but `edinburghfringe.js` had already existed since the 2026-06-22
  extractor restructure; the PR that closed it,
  [#881](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/pull/881),
  added a second recorded page, hardening an extractor that was already
  shipping, not new site support. Excluded from the local/civic-skew count
  below for that reason (it isn't a new-host demand signal), but it is a real
  use of the same form, filed by the same owner — the channel's only
  documented user treats it as a general-purpose "make this extractor better"
  form as much as a "this site doesn't work" one.

## Pain points to track (hypotheses — verify with real feedback as it arrives)

- Extraction misses or gets a field wrong on a page with unusual markup — the
  weekly
  [`generic-extractor-improvements`](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/blob/main/.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/generic-extractor-improvements/task.md)
  task (named `fallback-extractor-improvements` until the 2026-07-26 restructure
  retired the "fallback" vocabulary) is the engineering mechanism that narrows
  this over time; this wiki tracks it from the *user* side (which misses actually
  get reported/matter).
- Timezone correctness on pages that don't declare one clearly — see the
  unanimity rule in the contract header of
  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js` (a zone is emitted only
  when two independent page-declared hints agree, otherwise none). The
  `technicalGotchas.md` this line cited until 2026-07-26 was superseded when that
  doc was folded into the gcec pack; the rule did **not** move into that pack's
  RULES.md, it lives in the source file's own header. A wrong `ctz` is a
  trust-breaking failure mode worth watching from the user's perspective — and
  because the contract refuses to guess, the *user-visible* failure is usually a
  **missing** timezone rather than a wrong one, so the complaint shape to expect
  in feedback is "it didn't set the timezone", not "it set the wrong time".
- No support yet for calendars other than Google Calendar (see Market's open
  question on Outlook/ICS) — track whether this actually blocks real users or is
  a hypothetical gap.
- **A site that blocks automated fetching stays unsupported indefinitely**, and
  the user is never told why. Verified 2026-08-09 on `axs.com` and
  `bandsintown.com` (see the reported-demand section above): the request path
  needs a captured copy of the page to write a test case against, and a site
  that returns HTTP 403 to datacenter IPs never yields one. This is a distinct
  pain point from "unusual markup" above — the extraction is not the hard part.
- **Reporting a miss requires a GitHub account.** The in-product "Suggest
  Correction" / "open an issue" affordances open the repo's prefilled issue form
  (`extension/events-popup/source-request-view.js`), so a user without a GitHub
  login has no way to report at all. Watch whether this is what keeps outside
  reports at zero.

## Open questions

- Do real users cite privacy/permissions as a *reason for choosing* a lightweight
  extension, or is it a latent preference they don't act on? (The permission-risk
  data above is industry-wide, not this extension's own user feedback.)
- ~~Which extraction misses actually get reported vs. silently tolerated — i.e.
  which sites matter enough to users to warrant a dedicated extractor?~~
  **Answered in the negative, 2026-08-09**: all 13 `extractor-request` issues to
  date are the repo owner's, so *no* miss has ever been reported by an outside
  user. The question that replaces it is the one below, about the channel.
- **Is the GitHub-account gate what keeps outside reports at zero?** The only
  report path is a prefilled GitHub issue form (see the reported-demand section).
  Worth deciding whether a no-account channel is worth building, or whether the
  zero simply reflects a small install base — the two are indistinguishable from
  inside the repo, and install counts are still unobtainable (see
  [`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md)'s standing open question).
  Surfaced 2026-08-09.
- **Is the local/civic skew in reported demand a property of the demand or of
  the single reporter?** Nine of thirteen site requests now name Israeli hosts
  (up from eight of twelve — see the 2026-09-20 refresh below). If it is real,
  it argues the product's edge is small venue and civic sites rather than the
  ticketing majors an AI competitor covers by default; if it is just one
  person's browsing, it should not steer extractor priorities. Only outside
  reports can separate the two. Surfaced 2026-08-09.
- Does the lack of non-Google-Calendar support actually block real users? (Pairs
  with Market's `.ics`-export note.)
- On timezone, which complaint shape actually shows up — "wrong time" or "no
  timezone at all"? The refusal-to-guess contract predicts the latter dominates;
  no real feedback yet either way (surfaced 2026-07-26).

## Sources

design decisions (`dev/procedures/highLevelDesign.md`,
`dev/requirements/requirements.md`) and general competitor positioning (see
`../Competitors/README.md`'s sources) — not yet from direct user research. Flag this
clearly until real user feedback (reviews, issues, support requests) backs a
